title: A stranger in the world
hookLine: be in this world like a stranger or a traveler: step back, or walk the road with others?
tomorrow: who would actually love reaching the end of the road?

cards: Carry-on only. Some travelers swear by it: one bag, nothing checked, out of the airport while everyone else waits at the carousel. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once gave packing advice for a whole life.
He took a young companion, Abdullah ibn Umar, by the shoulder and said: be in this world as if you were a stranger, or a traveler passing through. How much to pack? Not much.
But what does traveling light look like on an ordinary Tuesday? Muslims have answered that in two ways.

teach.h: BE A STRANGER, OR A TRAVELER.
teach.b: The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari, and Imam Nawawi placed it in his collection called the Forty Hadith.

Ibn Umar added his own advice after it: in the evening, don't wait for the morning; in the morning, don't wait for the evening; take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death.

One view leans toward stepping back. A stranger doesn't sink deep roots in a town he's leaving, so keep few things, avoid what pulls you in, choose quiet. Muslims drawn to zuhd, doing without, live close to this.
At its best, it frees the heart: nothing to defend, nothing to lose. The other view says the traveler still walks through the town. He buys bread, greets people, helps the one who's stuck.

It points to a report in Tirmidhi: the believer who mixes with people and bears their harm patiently is better than the one who keeps away. At its best, this keeps the stranger kind and useful instead of aloof.
Both agree on the bag: carry less, and don't mistake the road for home.
They differ on how much of the road to walk with others.
One detail worth repeating: the advice came with a hand on the shoulder.

how: Muslims often quote this hadith (number 40 in Imam Nawawi's Forty Hadith) when talking about zuhd, holding the world lightly; some live very simply, while others stress staying among people and serving them.

games.q: what does “a stranger in the world” mean?
o: a newcomer who has just moved to a different country
staying polite but distant from the people around you
living like a traveler: carrying little, not settling in

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: be like a stranger or a traveler
in the evening, don't wait for morning
doing without, holding the world lightly
mix with people and bear their harm

s: 'be a stranger in the world' means Muslims should keep away from people
one strong view says the traveler still walks with others; a report in Tirmidhi praises mixing with people and bearing their harm.
Ibn Umar added: in the evening, don't wait for the morning
and: take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death.
the stepping-back view and the walking-with-others view disagree about carrying less
both agree on the bag. they differ on how much of the road to walk with others.

games.q: your study group splits. one friend says being 'a stranger in the world' means deleting social apps and skipping most parties. you lean the other way. what's her view's best case?
o: owning and joining less frees the heart from what pulls it.
the world is evil, so any contact with it is a sin.
a stranger isn't responsible for anyone, so stay out of it.
games.why: at its best, stepping back frees the heart: nothing to defend, nothing to lose. the other view's best case: stay kind and useful on the road.

practice: Look at what you carry every day: your bag, your pockets, the apps on your phone's first screen. Choose one thing in there you could set down for good.
Hold it, or rest your eyes on it, for a few slow breaths, and then put it to one side.

wordCard.voice: A stranger in the world: living like a traveler passing through. Carrying little, and never mistaking the road for home.

orig.note: Arabic: a stranger, someone far from home; the word in the hadith.

carryVoice: Two words to take along: just passing, with a light bag and kindness for the people on the road. Goodnight.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6416: be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler, with Ibn Umar's added advice; also hadith 40 of al-Nawawi's Forty Hadith
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2507 (also Ibn Majah 4032): the believer who mixes with people and is patient with their harm is better than the one who does not
